9.t: Working with data: C–G pairs and stability
q: Calculate the gradient of the line for 0.2 mol dm⁻³ salt. Include units.
Explain the effect of C–G content on the melting temperature.
A C–G pair is held by three hydrogen bonds, an A–T pair by two. More C–G means more bonds to break, so more heat energy is needed.
Suggest why DNA separates at a lower temperature in low salt.
The phosphate groups are negatively charged and repel each other. Positive ions in the salt shield these charges; with fewer ions the strands repel more and separate more easily.
A DNA sample melts at 92 °C in 0.2 mol dm⁻³ salt. Estimate the percentage of adenine.
92 °C means about 55% C–G, so A + T is about 45% and A is about 22 to 23%.
A student claims that bacteria in hot springs survive because their DNA is rich in C–G. Evaluate this claim.

High C–G does raise the melting temperature, but even 70% C–G melts at 98 °C, and many heat-loving species have ordinary C–G. Other features (DNA-binding proteins, salts, supercoiling) must also matter, so the claim is only partly supported.
